newsitem.title: FRANCE: French underwater explorer Cousteau dies, aged 87.
newsitem.headline: French underwater explorer Cousteau dies, aged 87.

text.p: Veteran French oceanographer Jacques-Yves Cousteau, who popularised underwater exploration with prize-winning films, died on Wednesday aged 87, his foundation said.

A brief statement from the Equipe Cousteau foundation said: "Captain Jacques-Yves Cousteau has gone to the world of silence this Wednesday, June 25, 1997. A great tribute will be paid to him in Paris."
It said Cousteau's widow would make a statement to the media in the late morning. It did not give the cause of death.

In his trademark sea-blue tunic and red beret, Cousteau became a familiar figure through books and films, particularly the U.S.-sponsored television series "The Undersea World of Jacques-Yves Cousteau," first broadcast in 1965.

A member of the prestigious French Academy since 1988 and regularly voted one of France's most popular men, he campaigned against marine pollution and joined international protests against France's nuclear testing in the South Pacific in 1995.
From the Antarctic to the Amazon and the depths of the oceans, Cousteau won a world-wide reputation as a champion of the environment.

He won a string of prizes for his films, including three Oscars and three awards at the Cannes film festival. Cousteau toured the world in the Calypso, a converted British minesweeper equipped with a marine laboratory.
He laid the basis for his career in 1943, when he and a French engineer built the first operational skin-diving suit, freeing divers from heavy helmets and allowing them to swim with flippers.
